title: Adobe Commerce to Shopify Plus Migration Playbook: 9 Phased Steps
summary: A phased Adobe Commerce to Shopify Plus migration playbook: data export sequencing, ERP re-integration, redirect strategy and 90-day post-launch stabilisation.
body_markdown:
**Quick Answer:** A successful Adobe Commerce to Shopify Plus migration runs in dependency order: audit and classify features, export customers then products then orders, re-integrate ERP via webhooks, build a redirect map from server logs, rehearse cutover twice, then freeze features for 30 days post-launch.


---


Success, eighteen months after a replatform, looks boring. Orders flow into the ERP without a nightly reconciliation call. Organic revenue is at or above pre-launch levels. Your developer invoices are for features, not for patching a 2.4.x security release at 2am. Nobody on the commercial team remembers which fiscal quarter the cutover happened in.


That is the only outcome worth planning for, and most Adobe Commerce to Shopify Plus migration playbook documents you'll find online don't work backwards from it. They work forwards from a data export checklist, which is why so many migrations land on time and then bleed for two quarters — orders stuck in a middleware queue, B2B customers unable to see their contract pricing, 40% of long-tail category URLs 404ing because nobody mapped layered navigation.

This playbook is written from the perspective of the person who has to answer for that. It sequences the work in the order the dependencies actually resolve, with specific attention to the three things that cause the overruns I see most often across Asia-Pacific merchants: ERP re-integration, redirect coverage on faceted URLs, and multi-entity tax and currency setup across Hong Kong, Singapore, Taiwan and Australia.


## Prerequisites: What Must Be True Before You Start


Skipping this section is how a 12-week project becomes a 30-week project. Ask Phill's 2026 migration analysis puts the realistic range at 8 to 24 weeks and €20,000 to €700,000+ depending on catalogue and integration complexity — a spread that wide is almost entirely explained by how much of the following was settled before kickoff.


### Commercial and contractual readiness


Know your Adobe renewal date and your notice period. Adobe Commerce licences are typically annual with auto-renewal, and the single most expensive migration mistake is paying for an overlapping year because the cutover slipped past the notice window. Build the project plan backwards from renewal minus 60 days, not forwards from today.


On the other side, Shopify Plus publicly starts at USD 2,300/month on a one-year term (Shopify's published Plus pricing), with variable rates for higher GMV. Model total cost of ownership including apps — most enterprise migrations land on 8 to 15 paid apps, and that app stack is frequently 30–50% of the recurring platform cost. If you only compare licence line items you will mis-forecast.


### Technical readiness


You need three artefacts before anyone touches a theme:


- **A full database snapshot and a frozen staging copy of production.** Every export you run must be reproducible from the same point-in-time snapshot. Running exports against live production on different days produces data that will never reconcile.
- **An integration register.** Every system that reads from or writes to Adobe Commerce, with its direction, transport (REST, SOAP, SFTP, direct DB), frequency, and the business process that breaks if it stops. In my experience this register is always longer than the client thinks — there is invariably a finance spreadsheet pulling from a read-replica that nobody documented.
- **A URL inventory.** Server logs plus Google Search Console plus a full crawl. Not just the sitemap — the sitemap is the subset of URLs you intended to have.


### Organisational readiness


Name one person with authority to say "we are not rebuilding that." Adobe Commerce estates accumulate a decade of bespoke logic, and roughly 20–30% of it is no longer used by anyone. Without a single decision-maker, every unused feature gets rebuilt "just in case," and that is where scope creep lives.

## Step 1: Audit the Adobe Commerce Estate and Classify Every Feature


### Separate platform features from business logic


Adobe Commerce ships functionality that Shopify Plus delivers differently rather than not at all. Multi-store setups become Shopify Markets or separate stores. Customer groups become B2B company locations and catalogues. Cart price rules become automatic discounts plus Shopify Functions. Classify each item as *native equivalent* , *app required* , *custom development* , or *retire* .


The retire column is the one that saves budget. Run a usage query before you decide. For cart price rules:


```text
1  SELECT   r  .  rule_id  ,   r  .  name  ,   r  .  is_active  ,     COUNT  (  o  .  entity_id  )     AS   uses    2   FROM   salesrule r    3   LEFT     JOIN   salesrule_coupon c   ON   c  .  rule_id   =   r  .  rule_id    4   LEFT     JOIN   sales_order o   ON   o  .  coupon_code   =   c  .  code    5      AND   o  .  created_at   >   DATE_SUB  (  NOW  (  )  ,     INTERVAL     12     MONTH  )     6   GROUP     BY   r  .  rule_id    7   ORDER     BY   uses   ASC  ;
```


Anything with zero uses in twelve months is a conversation, not a requirement.


### Quantify the extension debt


List every third-party module with its vendor, version, and last update date. For each, decide whether the Shopify equivalent is an app, a Shopify Function, or nothing. Adobe's move toward Edge Delivery Services and a new storefront architecture (documented on Adobe Business and Experience League) means some of your existing frontend extensions are heading for rework regardless of whether you migrate — factor that into the do-nothing baseline. The honest comparison is not "Shopify cost vs zero," it's "Shopify cost vs Adobe renewal plus the storefront rework plus ongoing patching."


### Map the B2B surface area honestly


If you run dealer or wholesale channels, this is the step that determines feasibility. Shopify Plus B2B (native company accounts, price lists, payment terms, and B2B catalogues documented at shopify.dev) covers a large share of common requirements, but specific patterns — multi-level approval chains, credit limit enforcement against a live ERP balance, quote negotiation workflows — need apps or custom work. Write down each requirement as a user story before anyone gives you a timeline.


A manufacturer selling through a regional dealer network that we worked with had 14 customer groups in Adobe Commerce. On inspection, 11 of them resolved to three price lists plus a location-level flag. That kind of simplification is normal, and finding it early is worth more than any tooling choice you make later.

## Step 2: Sequence the Data Export in Dependency Order


The single most common technical failure in an Adobe Commerce to Shopify Plus migration playbook is exporting everything in parallel and then discovering that order records reference customer IDs that don't exist yet, or variants that were merged during product cleanup.


### The correct order is: customers, products, then orders


Export and import in this sequence, validating each stage before starting the next:


1. **Customers** — including addresses, tax exemptions, company assignments, and accepts-marketing flags. Customers must exist before orders can reference them.
2. **Products** — simple products first, then configurables mapped to Shopify variants, then bundles and grouped products (which have no direct Shopify equivalent and need a bundling app or a product-set pattern).
3. **Collections and content** — category tree flattened to collections, CMS pages, blog posts.
4. **Orders** — historical orders imported as-is, unfulfilled orders handled separately (see Step 7).
5. **Metafields, reviews, loyalty balances, gift card balances** — last, because they attach to objects created above.


### Handle the configurable-to-variant problem early


Adobe Commerce configurables support unlimited attributes. Shopify supports up to three option names per product and 2,000 variants per product (current limits documented at shopify.dev). Any product with four or more configurable axes needs a decision: collapse an axis into a metafield, split into multiple products, or use a variant-expansion app. Count your offenders with a query against` catalog_product_super_attribute` before you promise anything.


A pragmatic export shape for products looks like this — use Matrixify or a custom extractor, but normalise to Shopify's expected headers rather than Adobe's:


```text
1  Handle,Title,Vendor,Type,Tags,Option1 Name,Option1 Value,Option2 Name,Option2 Value,Variant SKU,Variant Price,Variant Inventory Qty,Variant Barcode,Image Src,Metafield: custom.legacy_entity_id    2  mens-wool-coat,Men's Wool Coat,Northfield,Outerwear,"aw25,wool",Size,M,Colour,Navy,NF-WC-M-NV,2480,14,4712345678901,https://cdn.example.com/wc-navy.jpg,1842
```


That` legacy_entity_id` metafield matters. Keep the Adobe entity ID on every product, variant, and customer you import. It is how you reconcile, how you debug, and how your ERP mapping survives the first month.


### Decide how much order history to bring


Importing ten years of orders is expensive in time and provides limited value. Most merchants need 24 months live in Shopify for customer service and returns, with the full history retained in a read-only archive or the data warehouse. Be specific: if your returns window is 90 days and your loyalty programme looks back 12 months, 24 months is generous. Agree this with finance in writing, because "we assumed you were bringing everything" is a classic post-launch argument.


## Step 3: Rebuild the Storefront Against Real Data


### Build theme-first, not design-first


Start from Dawn or a well-maintained Online Store 2.0 theme and work in sections. The temptation is to recreate the Adobe storefront pixel-for-pixel; resist it. You are inheriting a decade of layout decisions made around Magento's template constraints. Baymard Institute's ongoing e-commerce UX research consistently finds large usability gaps in enterprise checkout and product pages — a replatform is the cheapest moment you will ever have to fix them.


Work locally with the Shopify CLI so your theme is version-controlled:


```text
1  shopify theme dev --store your-store.myshopify.com    2  shopify theme push --unpublished --theme "Migration RC1"    3  shopify theme pull --theme-id 123456789 --only sections/
```


### Replace layered navigation deliberately


Adobe Commerce layered navigation generates faceted URLs. Shopify's native filtering uses Storefront Filtering with URL parameters, and the standard search-and-discovery app covers most cases. The decision you must make explicitly: which facet combinations deserve an indexable landing page as a collection, and which should be parameter-only and canonicalised. Pick the top facet URLs by organic landing-page sessions over the last 12 months and build those as real collections. Everything else becomes a parameter.


### Port metafields and structured content


Anything that lived in a custom EAV attribute becomes a metafield with a defined definition. Define them with types — not everything as` single_line_text_field` — because typed metafields give you validation and better theme ergonomics:


```text
1  mutation {    2    metafieldDefinitionCreate(definition: {    3      name: "Care instructions",    4      namespace: "custom",    5      key: "care_instructions",    6      type: "rich_text_field",    7      ownerType: PRODUCT    8    }) { createdDefinition { id } userErrors { message } }    9  }
```

## Step 4: Re-Integrate ERP, POS and Fulfilment


This is where APAC migrations overrun. Not the catalogue — the integrations. A merchant with 40,000 SKUs and one clean ERP connector migrates faster than a merchant with 3,000 SKUs and six point-to-point integrations held together by cron jobs.


### Rebuild as event-driven, not polling


Adobe Commerce integrations are typically polling-based: a scheduled job queries for new orders every N minutes. Shopify gives you webhooks, and you should use them. Register topics for` orders/create` ,` orders/updated` ,` refunds/create` ,` inventory_levels/update` , and` fulfillments/create` , with a queue behind them.


```text
1  curl -X POST "https://your-store.myshopify.com/admin/api/2025-01/webhooks.json" \    2    -H "X-Shopify-Access-Token: $TOKEN" \    3    -H "Content-Type: application/json" \    4    -d '{"webhook":{"topic":"orders/create","address":"https://mw.example.com/hooks/orders","format":"json"}}'
```


Two non-negotiables: verify the HMAC on every payload, and make your handler idempotent on` X-Shopify-Order-Id` . Shopify retries failed deliveries, and duplicate order creation in an ERP is a finance incident, not a bug ticket.


### Use bulk operations for anything above 1,000 records


For nightly inventory and price syncs, don't loop the REST API. Shopify's GraphQL bulk operations run asynchronously and return a JSONL file:


```text
1  mutation {    2    bulkOperationRunQuery(query: """    3      { products { edges { node { id handle    4          variants { edges { node { id sku inventoryQuantity price } } } } } }    5    """) { bulkOperation { id status } userErrors { message } }    6  }
```


Shopify ships a new Admin API version each quarter and supports each for a minimum of 12 months (per the shopify.dev API versioning policy). Build your integration to pin a version explicitly and put the quarterly review in someone's calendar. Teams that don't do this discover it 11 months later, at speed.


### Map multi-entity tax, currency and markets


For merchants operating across Hong Kong, Singapore, Taiwan, Malaysia and Australia, this is the step that needs a finance stakeholder in the room. Adobe store views are not a one-to-one match for Shopify Markets. Decide per region whether you need:


- A **market** within one store (shared catalogue, localised pricing, local domain) — right for most of APAC where product ranges overlap.
- A **separate store** — right when the legal entity, ERP company code, or product catalogue genuinely differs, or where a local payment gateway cannot be attached to a shared store.


Singapore GST, Australian GST with low-value-import thresholds, and Taiwan's e-invoice (eGUI) requirements each have specific handling. Taiwan e-invoicing in particular typically needs a local provider integration, not a global tax app. Scope it as a distinct workstream and not as a line under "tax configuration."


### Keep POS and online inventory in one source of truth


If you run physical retail across multiple markets — a scenario common among Greater China jewellery, fashion and catering groups — decide before launch whether Shopify or the ERP owns inventory truth. Both answers work. Having no answer produces oversells in week two. Put the decision in the integration register, with the reconciliation frequency and the tolerance threshold that triggers an alert.


## Step 5: Build the Redirect Map Before You Touch DNS


### Crawl, don't guess


Google's own site-move documentation is unambiguous: when URLs change, every old URL needs a 301 to the closest equivalent, and redirects should stay in place for at least a year (Google Search Central, "Site move with URL changes"). The practical implication is that your redirect map must be built from a crawl of what exists, not from a sitemap of what you think exists.


Source your URL list from four places and deduplicate:


```text
1  # 1. Server access logs — real crawled and clicked URLs    2  awk '{print $7}' access.log* | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn > logs_urls.txt    3
4  # 2. Search Console performance export (all pages, 16 months)    5  # 3. Full site crawl (Screaming Frog / Sitebulb)    6  # 4. Backlink export (Ahrefs / Semrush) — URLs with external equity
```


Prioritise by sessions and referring domains. In a typical enterprise catalogue, 5,000–15,000 URLs carry essentially all of the organic value, and tens of thousands of faceted URLs carry almost none — but the ones that do carry value are usually faceted.


### Know Shopify's URL prefixes and plan around them


Shopify enforces path prefixes:` /products/` ,` /collections/` ,` /pages/` ,` /blogs/` . Your Adobe URLs almost certainly don't use them. That means a near-total URL change, and no amount of configuration avoids it. Upload redirects in bulk via the Admin API or a CSV:


```text
1  Redirect from,Redirect to    2  /mens-outerwear/wool-coat-navy.html,/products/mens-wool-coat?variant=navy    3  /mens-outerwear.html,/collections/mens-outerwear    4  /catalogsearch/result/?q=wool+coat,/search?q=wool+coat
```


For patterns that resist one-to-one mapping — thousands of faceted combinations — handle them with a catch-all rule at the edge rather than individual entries. If you front the store with Cloudflare, a regex rule covering` /*?dir=asc&order=*` patterns is cheaper to maintain than 8,000 redirect rows.


### Test the map against live traffic before cutover


Run your full old-URL list against a staging domain and assert that every one returns a single 301 to a 200. No chains, no loops, no redirects to collections that return empty. Automate it:


```text
1  while read url; do    2    code=$(curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" -I "https://staging.example.com$url")    3    final=$(curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{url_effective}" -L "https://staging.example.com$url")    4    echo "$url,$code,$final"    5  done < old_urls.txt > redirect_audit.csv
```


Also carry over structured data, hreflang (critical for multi-market APAC stores), and canonical logic. And confirm that your Shopify` robots.txt.liquid` customisations don't block the paths your paid media team relies on.

## Step 6: Rehearse the Cutover at Least Twice


### Run a full dress rehearsal on a clone


A rehearsal means: restore the production snapshot, run every import script end-to-end in sequence, point the integrations at a sandbox ERP, and time each stage. You are measuring two things — total elapsed time and which stage is the bottleneck. Large catalogue imports and image migrations are usually the long pole, and images are the one thing you can do early and incrementally.


### Define the delta-sync window


Between your final full export and go-live, the Adobe store keeps taking orders and changing stock. You need an explicit plan for that delta:


- **Catalogue delta** — re-export products modified since the snapshot, import as an update-only pass keyed on SKU.
- **Customer delta** — same, keyed on email.
- **Order delta** — usually the cleanest approach is to stop taking orders on Adobe at a defined time, let in-flight orders fulfil on the old system, and start Shopify clean. Open orders mid-fulfilment should be completed on Adobe, not migrated.
- **Inventory** — a single authoritative sync from the ERP immediately after DNS switch.


### Write the runbook with named owners and rollback gates


The runbook is a timestamped list of steps, each with an owner, an expected duration, a verification check, and a rollback trigger. For example: *T+0:30 — DNS updated (Owner: infra). Verify:*` dig` *returns Shopify IP from three regions. Rollback trigger: checkout error rate >2% for 10 minutes → revert A record.*


Schedule the cutover for your lowest-traffic window with the whole team available, and avoid the 48 hours before any major sales period. In APAC that means working around 11.11, 12.12, Chinese New Year and local equivalents — and remembering that your Hong Kong, Sydney and London stakeholders are in three different working days.


## Step 7: Validate Before and After the Switch


### Transactional UAT with real money


Before launch, place live test orders — real cards, real amounts, refunded afterwards — across every payment method, every market, and every fulfilment path. Confirm each one appears correctly in the ERP, generates the right tax treatment, triggers the right notification email in the right language, and refunds cleanly. Test B2B separately: a company location on net-30 terms placing an order against a price list behaves nothing like a retail checkout.


### Instrumentation parity


Verify analytics, consent management, server-side tagging, and ad platform conversion tracking fire in Shopify's checkout environment — which uses Checkout Extensibility and Web Pixels rather than arbitrary script injection. Script tags and checkout.liquid customisations do not carry over. If your attribution relies on a custom checkout script, that is a rebuild, and it needs to be validated before launch, not after.


### The first-72-hours watch list


Monitor, hourly at first: 404 rate by URL pattern, checkout completion rate versus pre-launch baseline, webhook failure count, ERP order queue depth, inventory variance, and Search Console crawl errors. Keep the Adobe environment running in read-only mode for at least 30 days. You will need it for a reconciliation question you haven't thought of yet.

## Step 8: Stabilise Across 30, 60 and 90 Days


### Days 1–30: fix, don't build


Freeze new feature work. The backlog in the first month is entirely defects, redirect gaps, and integration edge cases. Triage daily. Resist the pressure to ship the new loyalty programme while order sync is still producing exceptions.


Expect organic fluctuation. Google's documentation on site moves notes that changes take time to be fully processed and that temporary ranking fluctuation is normal; plan communications with your CMO accordingly, and have the Search Console data to distinguish "Google is reprocessing" from "we broke something."


### Days 31–60: close the data loop


Reconcile finance. Match order counts, revenue, tax collected, and refunds between Shopify, the ERP, and the payment gateway for every day since launch. Mismatches found in month two are cheap. Mismatches found at year-end close are not.


This is also when you retire the temporary scaffolding: remove one-off import scripts from production, revoke the API credentials used for migration, and document the final integration architecture against the register you built in the prerequisites.


### Days 61–90: start capturing the upside


Now build. Shopify Functions for discount and shipping logic, Shopify Flow for operational automation, headless or hydrogen experiments if the roadmap calls for it. The business case for migration almost always rests on faster iteration — Shopify's own platform comparison claims migrations to Shopify run 25% faster on average than migrations to Adobe Commerce — and that only pays off if you actually iterate. A merchant who migrates and then ships nothing for six months has converted a capital cost into no benefit.


## Common Mistakes and How to Troubleshoot Them


### Orders duplicating in the ERP


Symptom: finance reports the same order twice. Cause: webhook retries hitting a non-idempotent handler, or both a webhook and a polling job writing the same record. Fix: dedupe on Shopify order ID at the integration layer, and remove the polling job entirely once webhooks are verified. Never run both as "belt and braces" — that is the cause, not the safety net.


### Inventory oversells in week two


Symptom: items sell online that retail already sold. Cause: no agreed source of truth, or a sync interval longer than your fastest sales velocity. Fix: declare the authority, shorten the interval for fast-moving SKUs, and configure continue-selling-when-out-of-stock only where you genuinely can backorder.


### Organic traffic drops more than expected and doesn't recover


Symptom: a decline beyond the expected short-term dip, persisting past 6–8 weeks. First check the redirect audit against Search Console's "Not found (404)" report — the gap is almost always faceted URLs or paginated category pages that weren't in the sitemap. Second, check canonical tags on filtered collections. Third, check that a staging` noindex` didn't ship to production. That last one sounds amateurish; it happens on experienced teams, every year.


### B2B customers can't see their pricing


Symptom: logged-in wholesale accounts see retail prices. Cause: customers imported as retail customers rather than attached to a company location, or a price list assigned at the company level when the account structure needs it at the location level. Fix: audit the company-location-to-price-list mapping; this is almost never a theme problem even though it presents as one.


### Variants silently dropped during import


Symptom: SKU count in Shopify is lower than in Adobe. Cause: duplicate option-value combinations, products exceeding option or variant limits, or SKUs with trailing whitespace. Fix: reconcile on the` legacy_entity_id` metafield you set in Step 2, which is exactly why you set it.


### Scope creep via "while we're in there"


Symptom: the timeline slips in two-week increments with no single large cause. This is the most common overrun pattern across every migration I've been involved with, and the only reliable fix is structural: a written scope, a named decision-maker, and a parked-items list that the business can see. Everything requested after kickoff goes to the parked list and gets built in the days 61–90 window. The discipline is unpopular for three months and vindicated by month six.


### Expecting a downloadable template to do the work


People search for an Adobe Commerce to Shopify Plus migration playbook PDF, a GitHub repo, or a free template — and they exist, and they're useful as checklists. But no template knows your integration register, your renewal date, or whether Taiwan e-invoicing is in scope. Use templates for coverage; use your own audit for sequencing.

## Where This Is Heading


The replatform decision is narrowing. Adobe's direction of travel — Edge Delivery Services, a new storefront architecture, an increasingly composable posture — makes Adobe Commerce a stronger fit for organisations with in-house engineering capacity and genuinely unusual commercial logic. Shopify's direction — native B2B, Functions, Markets, Checkout Extensibility — makes it a stronger fit for brands whose competitive advantage is merchandising and speed rather than platform architecture. Those are different businesses, and the honest answer is that some merchants should stay.


For Asia-Pacific merchants specifically, two forces will shape the next few years of this decision. The first is cross-border: as Hong Kong, Singapore and Australian brands sell more directly into each other's markets and into the US and EU, multi-market tax, currency and compliance handling stops being an edge case and becomes the core requirement. The second is operating model. Global brands using Asia as an operations hub, and APAC brands scaling outward, both increasingly want a platform their regional team can change without a release train — which is a staffing argument as much as a technology one.


Whatever you choose, the sequence in this Adobe Commerce to Shopify Plus migration playbook holds: audit before you export, export in dependency order, integrate before you launch, redirect before you touch DNS, and spend the first 30 days fixing rather than building. The platform choice matters less than the discipline of the sequence.
